title: Ulysses
author: James Joyce
openingText: Stately, plump Buck Mulligan came up from the stairhead, carrying a bowl of shaving lather with a mirror and razor laid crosswise on top. A yellow dressing gown, untied, floated gently behind him in the mild morning air. He held the bowl up high and chanted:
about:
On Thursday, June 16, 1904, Leopold Bloom fries himself a kidney for breakfast in Dublin. He sells newspaper advertising. His day takes him to a funeral, a newspaper office and Davy Byrne's pub for a Gorgonzola sandwich. Elsewhere in the city, young Stephen Dedalus teaches a history lesson and grieves for his mother. The two men walk together late that night, and Bloom makes cocoa in his kitchen. The book closes with Molly Bloom lying awake beside her husband.

Joyce wrote Ulysses between 1914 and 1921, in Trieste, Zurich, and Paris. Sylvia Beach published it in Paris in 1922. An American court ruling in 1933 cleared the way for the authorised US edition in 1934; the first British edition appeared in 1936. The novel maps onto Homer's Odyssey episode by episode — Bloom is Odysseus, Stephen is Telemachus, Molly is Penelope — and Joyce developed schemes linking its eighteen episodes with locations, times, bodily organs and narrative techniques; not every category applies to every episode.

Ulysses is a major work of literary modernism and an unusually ambitious experiment in the English-language novel. It contains interior monologue, newspaper headlines, parodies of prose styles from Anglo-Saxon to Victorian magazine, a chapter in catechism, a chapter staged as a play. The technical detail of Dublin is so exact that Joyce claimed the city could be reconstructed from his book if it were destroyed. The novel's argument is that consciousness — ordinary, drifting, sexual, hungry, grieving consciousness — is the proper subject of fiction, and that an ad salesman's Thursday is as worth attending to as any king's homecoming.

angleCards.title: The formal experiment, episode by episode.
angleCards.text: Joyce reinvents his narrative technique for each of the eighteen episodes — interior monologue, catechism, newspaper parody, operatic libretto. I want to read Ulysses as a laboratory, noticing how each stylistic choice shapes what we know and feel about the same characters.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read episode by episode, following Joyce's formal experiment — how he changes the narrative technique with each chapter, and what each style reveals that the others couldn't.

angleCards.title: Bloom as the modern Odysseus.
angleCards.text: Homer's hero was cunning, brave, and exceptional. Joyce's hero buys a pork kidney. I want to read the Homeric parallels carefully — understanding what Joyce gains by mapping epic onto the mundane, and whether Bloom's decency is a form of heroism the ancient world couldn't have named.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read Leopold Bloom as the modern hero — understanding what it means that Joyce's Odysseus runs a newspaper ad and makes breakfast, and whether ordinariness is heroism in a different key.

angleCards.title: The father and the son.
angleCards.text: Stephen Dedalus is young, brilliant, and homeless in spirit. Leopold Bloom lost his son Rudy as an infant and has never recovered. Their paths converge on June 16 in a way that feels inevitable and doesn't resolve into anything neat. I want to follow what passes between them.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow the relationship between Stephen and Bloom — what each lacks that the other has, and whether their brief meeting amounts to something like the father-son bond neither of them has.

angleCards.title: Bloomsday as real autobiography.
angleCards.text: June 16, 1904 was the day James Joyce first walked out with Nora Barnacle — the woman he loved for the rest of his life. He chose it deliberately. I want to read the novel with that biographical key in hand, understanding what Joyce was doing by immortalising a particular Thursday in Dublin.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read June 16 as a real day — understanding the biographical fact that it was Joyce's first walk with Nora Barnacle, and what it means that he chose to make it the most scrutinised day in literary history.

cast.name: Leopold Bloom
cast.description: A thirty-eight-year-old Dublin advertising canvasser of Hungarian-Jewish descent. His son Rudy died at eleven days old, just over ten years before the novel opens, and he and his wife Molly have not had full sexual intercourse for more than ten years. He is curious, kind, scientifically minded, aware of his wife’s affair, and quietly grieving. He likes inner organs of beasts and fowls. He carries a potato in his pocket. The novel follows his consciousness through much of the day and into the night and finds, in the texture of one ordinary man's attention, a hero Homer could not have imagined.

cast.name: Stephen Dedalus
cast.description: A twenty-two-year-old schoolteacher and aspiring writer. Educated by Jesuits, he rejected a religious vocation. He returned from Paris when his mother fell ill and refused to pray at her deathbed. The novel inherits him from Joyce's earlier book A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man. He is brilliant, proud, articulate, broke, and spiritually homeless. He is Telemachus looking for a father he cannot quite name, and his own actual father — the drunken, sentimental Simon Dedalus — is everywhere in the city he is trying to leave.

cast.name: Molly Bloom
cast.description: Born Marion Tweedy in Gibraltar to Lunita Laredo and an Irish soldier, Major Tweedy, now a thirty-three-year-old professional singer in Dublin. She has spent the afternoon in bed with her concert promoter Blazes Boylan. She is sensual, sharp, funny, and intelligent in a way most of the men in the book do not register. Her closing monologue — eight long passages with almost no punctuation, drifting through memory, lust, marriage, and the line between them — is among the best-known passages in modernist fiction and the novel's last word on what consciousness is.

cast.name: Buck Mulligan
cast.description: A medical student who shares the Martello tower at Sandycove with Stephen and an English visitor. Mulligan opens the novel intoning a Latin parody of the Mass as he prepares to shave on the tower. He is brilliant, mocking, bawdy, and corrosive — a wit who uses comedy as a way of refusing to take anything seriously, including grief. Stephen cannot forgive his flippant remark about his mother being dead. Joyce based him on his real-life friend and rival Oliver St. John Gogarty.

cast.name: Blazes Boylan
cast.description: A Dublin man-about-town, concert promoter, and Molly's lover. Bloom knows the affair is happening; he knows Boylan has an appointment at his house at four o'clock; his awareness of the appointment follows him through the day. Boylan appears physically only briefly — ordering a basket of fruit on Grafton Street, riding a hansom — but his presence shadows Bloom’s thoughts through the day. He is what Bloom is not: confident, unreflective, sexually direct, and largely seen from the outside.

cast.name: Gerty MacDowell
cast.description: A young Dublin woman, slightly lame, sitting on Sandymount Strand at dusk while Bloom watches her from a distance during a fireworks display. The episode that contains her — Nausicaa — is written in the prose style of late-Victorian women's magazines, and her interior monologue runs in that register before the technique gives way to Bloom's. Joyce uses her to perform one of the novel's most exact stylistic experiments: a consciousness shaped almost entirely by the romantic fiction it has consumed, observed by another consciousness that is not.

acclaim.quote: I hold this book to be the most important expression which the present age has found.

whyItMatters.title: One Day, Eighteen Styles
whyItMatters.body: Joyce divided Ulysses into eighteen episodes and wrote each in a different prose register. The first three move between external narration and Stephen’s thoughts; the third, Proteus, is already demanding. After that, the techniques start coming apart on purpose. The Aeolus chapter is broken up by newspaper headlines and editorial parodies. The Oxen of the Sun episode runs a succession of English prose styles in chronological pastiche, from Anglo-Saxon alliterative verse through Bunyan and Sterne to a contemporary American religious tract. Circe is staged as a hallucinatory play with stage directions and impossible scene changes. Ithaca is written entirely in catechism — question and answer — describing Bloom's kitchen down to the volume of water in his teakettle and the trajectory of his urination. The form is the argument. A single ordinary day in a single city contains every register a writer could use, and no single register is enough. Its shifts of technique have become an influential model for later fiction.

whyItMatters.title: Ordinary Heroism
whyItMatters.body: Homer's Odysseus is a king, a warrior, a survivor of the Trojan War who washes up on Phaeacian shores naked and is recognized for who he is. Joyce's Odysseus is an ad salesman whose wife is sleeping with another man, who takes a bar of lemon soap with a promise to pay later, who eats a Gorgonzola sandwich alone in Davy Byrne's pub, who masturbates on Sandymount Strand watching a stranger during a fireworks display, who walks home in the small hours and offers the young poet a bed for the night. Stephen declines. Joyce's argument is that the patterns Homer found in heroic life — wandering, return, recognition, the offer of food to a stranger, the long delay before a husband and wife actually see each other again — are present in any sufficiently attentive Thursday in any sufficiently attended-to city. That attention to ordinary experience has helped shape later fiction.

whyItMatters.title: The Final Monologue
whyItMatters.body: Molly Bloom's closing chapter — episode eighteen, called Penelope — unfolds in eight long passages with almost no punctuation, almost no paragraph breaks, and almost no concession to the conventional reader. She lies awake beside Bloom in the small hours, drifting between memory and immediate physical sensation, working through her marriage, her lover that afternoon, her dead infant son, her childhood in Gibraltar, her sense of her own body and what it has been, her tenderness for her husband she rarely shows him, and finally the single afternoon on Howth Head years earlier when Bloom proposed and she said yes. The technique is Joyce's purest version of stream of consciousness, and the chapter ends — "yes I said yes I will Yes" — with one of the best-known affirmations in English-language fiction. Reading it is encountering the book's argument that consciousness is not what novels had assumed it was: not orderly, not single-tracked, not in sentences, not divisible into thought and sensation, but a continuous drift the prose has to invent a new technique to follow.
